Arrogance: “The fear of Hashem is hatred of evil, pride, arrogance and the evil way. (Mishlei 8)” This verse was mentioned by King Solomon, peace be upon him, in the name of Wisdom, says the Wisdom that one who possesses fear of Hashem will hate an evil person. “Hatred of evil” means hatred of an evil person, just as “And I am prayer” means a person of prayer. Since he is an evil person, it is a mitzvah to hate him, and that's why David said: “Do I not hate those who hate You, Hashem? (Tehilim 139)”, And Solomon said: “Those who forsake the Torah praise the wicked, but those who guard the Torah contend with them. (Mishlei 28)” For the righteous and the wicked are opposites; each hates the other. Every kind loves its own kind and hates its opposite. And Solomon said: “Men of blood hate the innocent. (Mishlei 29)” And he said: “The upright in way is an abomination to the wicked.” An evil person includes the evil traits mentioned: pride, arrogance, an evil path, and a perverse mouth. He mentioned the trait of pride first, for it is the most difficult of all traits, and whoever holds onto it is called an abomination of Hashem. The prophet Isaiah called it “a fading blossom,” as it says: “Woe to the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim, and the fading blossom of his glorious beauty. (Isaiah 28)” The verse explains: Woe to one who crowns pride; Israel held onto it and were intoxicated with it. This was said about the Ten Tribes who were at ease during the time of the Temple. He was prophesying punishment upon them. He called this trait a “fading blossom,” meaning a plant destined to fall. He said such a crown is fit to be trampled underfoot. “With feet shall be trampled the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim." The reason the trait is repeated “pride and arrogance”, may be explained as follows: pride has two aspects. One person is proud of his wisdom, of the uprightness of his conduct, of his good character traits, and of whatever superiority he believes he has over the people of his generation. Another is proud of his evil traits and of all acts of oppression and corruption. Both of these types are despised by the sages. It goes without saying that one who prides himself on deeds driven by the evil inclination is despised. But even one who prides himself on good deeds is included among those hated by the sages. This is the meaning of “pride and arrogance”: pride from the side of good, which is hatred of evil, and arrogance from the side of evil, which is the evil path, all of it I hate. For even if a person is righteous, and all his conduct is upright, and he performs all his deeds according to intellect and wisdom, it is not fitting for him to become proud of this; rather, he should humble himself. As it is said in the Midrash: Why were Israel compared to a vine? Just as a vine has large and small clusters, and the larger the cluster, the lower it bends, so too are Israel. It may also be said that this is the meaning of the verse stated regarding the Holy One, blessed be He: “For He has triumphed gloriously”, for they sang praise that He exalts Himself over good and exalts Himself over evil. He was a wall for Israel and a wall against Egypt. Pride is fitting for no one except Hashem alone, as it says, “Hashem reigns; He is clothed in majesty. Since the root of good and evil is one, the prophet therefore said, “He makes peace and creates evil,” and “I am Hashem Who does all these,” in order to remove from the hearts of heretics who claim that it is impossible for good and evil to emerge from one source. Therefore, the verse adds, “all these. He mentioned perversities because pride that stems from the evil path brings a person to speak twisted things. That pride forces him to deviate from the path of truth until he says things that ought not to be said. Our sages taught: Anyone who possesses arrogance deserves to be cut down like an Asherah tree. It is written here, “The tall of stature shall be cut down,” and it is written there, “You shall cut down their Asherim.” They further taught: Anyone who has arrogance, the Divine Presence laments over him, as it says, “And You know the haughty from afar.” Elsewhere they taught that leprosy is the punishment for the arrogant, as it says, “for swelling and for a scab,” and “swelling” implies elevation, as it says, “and upon all the high hills.” So too we find with Naaman, who was punished with leprosy because he was arrogant, as it says, “Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Aram, was a great man before his master”, meaning that he was haughty before his master. The severity of the prohibition of pride that we mentioned applies to a person’s conduct in speech and in actions between himself and his fellow. In speech, when he speaks haughtily, as it says, “He who raises his doorway seeks destruction.” The mouth is referred to as a doorway, for it is the entrance of the body as a gate is to a house. It is known that destruction is the punishment of the proud, as it says, “Before destruction comes pride,” and “A man’s pride shall bring him low. In actions, when he conducts himself in matters beyond his level, as David said, “I have not walked in great matters or in things too wondrous for me.” Needless to say, if one is proud regarding mitzvot between himself and the Omnipresent, honoring himself in some act of service, such as boasting of going to the synagogue with his lulav in hand and the like, thinking to honor himself while belittling other mitzvot whose transgression is more severe, the sin is grave and the punishment bitter. As we find with Shebna, who was a great official in the house of Hezekiah. He was proud in his performance of mitzvot and despised the sacrifices. According to our sages, he was a priest, as implied in the verse, “I will clothe him with your tunic.” Because he despised the sacrifices, he was punished, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, killed him. Regarding him it says, “The peg fastened in a secure place shall be removed. We also find with Issachar of Kefar Barkai, upon whom the Temple courtyard cried out because he was arrogant, honored himself, and desecrated sacred things. As our sages expounded in Pesachim, chapter “Makom Shenahagu,” that there were four cries that the courtyard cried out: First: “Depart from here, sons of Eli, who defiled the Sanctuary of Hashem. Again the courtyard cried: “Depart from here, Issachar of Kefar Barkai, who honors himself and desecrates the holy things of Heaven. Again the courtyard cried: “Lift up your heads, O gates, and let Ishmael ben Pabi, the disciple of Pinchas, enter and serve in the High Priesthood.” Again the courtyard cried: “Lift up your heads, O gates, and let Yochanan ben Narbai, the disciple of Barkai, enter and fill his belly from the sacred offerings.” The punishment of Issachar of Kefar Barkai is explained explicitly. Our sages said: The king and queen were sitting. The king said, “Kid meat is superior,” and the queen said, “Lamb is superior.” They said, “Let the High Priest decide, for he offers sacrifices all day.” They brought Issachar. He indicated with his hand that lamb is superior, for if kid were superior it would be offered as the daily offering. The king said, “Since he shows no fear of the monarchy, cut off his right hand.” Issachar gave a bribe, and they cut off his left hand. The king heard and said, “Let them return and cut off his right hand.” Rav Yosef said, “Blessed is the Merciful One who repaid Issachar in this world,” meaning it was better for him to receive his punishment in this world than in the World to Come.
Confession: "Against You alone have I sinned, and done what is evil in Your eyes; so that, etc." (Psalms 51:6). It is well-known that confession is a positive commandment which is in the Torah, as it is stated (Numbers 5:6-7), "When a man or woman shall commit any sin that men commit, to do a trespass against the Lord [...]. They shall confess the sins which they committed." And the content of confession is that they confess and say to the Holy One, blessed be He, "I have sinned before you." And the Rabbis, may their memory be blessed, expounded, "Once a person has confessed and said, 'I have sinned,' no angel is allowed anymore to touch him, as it is stated (Numbers 22:34), 'And Bilaam said to the angel of the Lord, "I have sinned because I did not know that you were standing in the way before me."'" And likewise do we find with the Jewish people that when they sinned by expressing evil speech against the manna, they confessed and said (Deuteronomy 21:7), "We sinned by speaking against the Lord and against you"; so the Holy One, blessed be He, forgave them immediately. And Moshe [too] prayed for them, as it is stated, "Moshe prayed on behalf of the people." And even with the wicked, confession atones. So once they have accepted their punishment and confession, they merit life in the world to come. For thus have we found with Aakhan, that he confessed and said (Joshua 7:20), "Indeed I have sinned against the Lord, God of Israel, and thus and thus have I done." And immediately after he confessed, Joshua said to him (Joshua 7:25), "What calamity you have brought upon us; the Lord will bring calamity upon you this day." And [the Rabbis], may their memory be blessed, expounded, "This day are you visited by calamity; but you are not visited by calamity for life in the world to come." And it is not necessary to say this about the Jewish people, for confession even atones for the [other] nations of the world. For this is what have we found [concerning] Adoni-bezek, a great king among the kings of the Canaanites; and there were seventy kings of Canaan with severed thumbs and big toes collecting scraps under his table. [Even so,] once he confessed and mentioned God, it was atoned for him. And that is that which is written at the beginning of Judges [Judges 1:5-7), "At Bezek, they encountered Adoni-bezek, engaged him in battle, and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him and captured him; and they cut off his thumbs and his big toes. And Adoni-bezek said, 'Seventy kings, with thumbs and big toes cut off, used to pick up scraps under my table; as I have done, so God has requited me.' They brought him to Jerusalem and he died there." What is of interest [here], that the verse mentioned his death in Jerusalem? Rather, it is to teach you that once he confessed and mentioned God, may He be blessed, in his confession, his death was atonement, since he accepted his punishment as being measure for measure.
Honoring Parents: Come and see how beloved the commandment of honoring father and mother is in front of the Holy One, blessed be He! As the Holy One, blessed be He, does not distinguish between the righteous and the evil [in this regard]. From where do we [know this]? From the evil Esau. Since he honored his father, the Holy One, blessed by He, gave him 'all this honor' [as] his reward. Rabbi Eliezer says, "Esau wept three tears, one from his right eye, one from his left eye and the third solidified and did not descend. When? At the time that Yitzchak blessed Yaakov, as it is stated (Genesis 27:38), 'and Esav raised his voice and wept.'" Come and see how much tranquility the Holy One, blessed be He, gave him [as a result]! As it is stated (Psalms 80:6), "You fed them tears for bread; You gave them a third of the tears to drink." It is not written, "three," but rather "a third," since the three tears were not complete. And if the Holy One, blessed be He, repaid this evil one because he honored his father, all the more is it with a righteous person who honors his elders. The Holy One, blessed be He, said, "Is there anyone who gave his father honor and I did not give him children?" The commandment of honor is the fifth of the Ten Commandments, and it seals the first tablet. As behold, the tablet began with, "I am," which is honoring the ultimate Farther, and ends with, "Honor," which is about the reproductive father. And the commandment of honoring [parents] only came for the honor of the ultimate Father. And in the same way as the reproductive father, who engenders the child, is called father; so too is the ultimate Father, who engendered the soul and blew it from His holy spirit, called father. And greater are the kindnesses of the ultimate Father towards His creatures than the kindnesses of the reproductive father towards his child. For so did David say (Psalms 29:10), "Though my father and mother abandon me, the Lord will take me in." And likewise did Isaiah mention (Isaiah 63:16), "Surely You are our Father; though Abraham regard us not, and Israel recognize us not, You, O Lord, are our Father; from of old, Your name is 'Our Redeemer.'" It is saying, we did not know Avraham in the exile of Egypt, nor Yaakov in the desert. For the forefathers had already gone. And if so, You are the supernal ultimate Father. From of old, Your name is "Our Redeemer," since You redeemed us from Egypt. And likewise did Moshe, peace be upon him, mention (Deuteronomy 32:6), "is He not your Father, who made you His; He who made you and established you?"
Rain: Isaiah, peace be upon him, said: O Lord, in their distress, they sought You; Your chastisement reduced them to anguished whispered prayer (Isaiah 26:16). For when the Jewish people are in distress, they seek Him with fasting and with prayer. For behold, it is well known that from the day that the Jewish people went into exile, they suffered from the illness of troubles more than any nation. And the rabbis, may their memory be blessed, expounded that when the teacher walks into the study hall with a whip in his hand, who worries? The one the way of which is to be hit. So too is the Jewish people accustomed to troubles from when they went into exile in [other] lands. So they have to worry more than the other nations when they see troubles spreading in the world; and all the more so when they see them coming towards them or spreading in them. And about this does Scripture say: May the Lord answer you in time of trouble, etc. (Psalms 20:2). There was no righteous person that encountered as many troubles as Jacob: The trouble with Laban, the trouble with Rachel, the trouble with Dinah, and the trouble with Joseph. And that is why Jacob is mentioned more than the other patriarchs. And they, may their memory be blessed, said, "The Holy One, blessed be He, only shakes up the world for the sake of the Jewish people." And the reason for that is so that they will move their hearts to repentance and pray before Him. And also explicit is that tragedies only come for the sake of the Jewish people, as it is stated: I wiped out nations, their corner towers are desolate, etc. And I thought that she would fear Me, would learn a lesson (Zephaniah 3:6-7). And this is correct — since the Holy One, blessed be He, chose the Jewish people more than other nations and they are the center of the world, it is fitting to sustain it or to destroy it on their account. Everything is according to their deeds. And they should not ascribe the thing to chance. As behold Scripture stated: And if you walk with Me haphazardly — meaning to say that when I shake up My world and initiate harsh decrees upon you; if you evaluate it and ascribe it to chance, like the way of the world, and that it is not with directed providence and with an intention known by Me — I will also walk with you [editor's correction: them] haphazardly (Leviticus 26:41). Meaning, I will continue and add more of that happenstance and allow the constellation to go on its path and not direct it at all, rather it shall all be by chance. And it also stated: And I will walk with you furiously haphazardly (Leviticus 26:28). It is as it is stated: So I poured out My wrath on them because (Ezekiel 36:18) they relate everything to chance.

When sufferings of chastisement come upon a person, he returns to the good. As the sages interpreted the Song of Songs, "Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and pleasant" - even when You bring upon me sufferings of chastisement, it is pleasant. Why? Because You return me thus to the good. Human repentance is never complete without suffering. Repentance is improving one's actions and character. It is not fasting and wearing sackcloth and wallowing in the dust and immersing in water while remaining soiled on the inside with sins and evil thoughts. And so said the prophet (Isaiah 58): "Do you call that a fast, A day when the LORD is favorable?" "No, this is the fast I desire: To unlock fetters of wickedness, And untie the cords of the yoke." [...] The intent of the Torah is that one should first cleanse oneself on the inside, casting out from one's heart the impurities of sin, and then return what one has taken unfairly or by violence, and ask forgiveness from one's friend. After immersing one's heart inwardly and doing all kinds of purification and cleansing oneself from sin, one should purify oneself also outwardly by fasting and immersing the body, and so on...
Passover: ... And on this the Torah says (Exodus 13:7) "there will not be seen and there will not be found" - it will not be seen b'maaseh (in action) and will not be found b'machshava (in thought), rather one should anul it in his heart. The mitzvot have 3 categories: mitzvot of speech, of the heart and of action, as it is written (Deuteronomy 30:14) "in your mouth and in your heart to do it". Comes the Torah (instructing us) to anul it in the heart, corresponding to the mitzvot which are dependent on the heart. Comes the 'kabbalah' (instructing us) to eradicate it from the house or to burn it, corresponding to the mitzvot of action. And to say 'kol chamira', corresponding to mitzvot of speech. In this way the 3 categories of mitzvot are fulfilled through the prohibition of chametz, teaching you that the prohibition of chametz incorporates all the mitzvot... Just as the 'kabbalah' comes (instructing us) to eradicate chametz and (livdok) to check the house in nooks and in cracks, so too we are obligated to search and check the chambers of our inner being for bad (machshavas) intentions and bad (hirhurim) thoughts. Just as bedikat chametz (checking for chametz) is not valid by sunlight, nor by moonlight, nor by the light of a torch, but only by the light of a candle, so too the bedikah (checking) of the yetzer hara must be by the light of the neshama (soul) which is called 'ner' (candle), this is what is written (Proverbs 20:27) "the candle of Hashem is the soul of man, which searches the chambers of one's inner being.
